title: The Imperial Standard
subtitle: Aurelian society and visual identity
summary: Navy, cream and polished brass; ministries built to last a century; serial numbers, forms that exist for a reason, and tea in a storm.
content:
> *"This institution expects to still exist in a hundred years."*
> — what Aurelian architecture is said to say to visitors

Everything Aurelian is meant to communicate the same few things: **order**, **scale**, **polish**, **standardisation** and **institutional authority**. A Vardic engine tells you who made it. An Aurelian one tells you which department is responsible for it, when it was last serviced, and where to order the replacement part.

This entry describes how the [Aurelian Empire](factions.html#aurelian-empire) looks and carries itself. For the history behind it, see [[the-aurelian-empire|The Aurelian Empire]]. For the faith that underwrites its sense of duty, see [[crowned-sun|The Crowned Sun]].

## Colours and Emblems

The Aurelian palette is **navy**, **cream**, **black** and **white**, set off by **polished brass**, **gold trim**, **dark wood** and **steel**. Imperial red appears sparingly, mostly in the crown.

The Empire's emblem gathers its favourite symbols into one device: a **crown**, a **sun** with compass points, an **anchor** and a wreath of **laurel**. The eight-pointed star of the compass recurs everywhere, on epaulettes, cuff trim, badges and banners.

![The flag of the Aurelian Empire](data/images/aurelian-empire-flag-dfc34225.jpg "The Aurelian flag: a crowned sun-and-compass device over an anchor, wreathed in laurel, on a cream cross over navy, with an eight-pointed star in each quarter. Look for the same crown, sun and star on badges, cuffs and ministry seals.")

## Built to Last a Hundred Years

Aurelian architecture favours **symmetry**, **monumental stone**, broad administrative buildings, naval institutions, formal plazas, columns, and interiors of polished floors, dark hardwood and brass fixtures. Even a minor customs house is built as if it expects to outlive everyone working in it, which is exactly the impression it is meant to give.

![An Aurelian capital and harbour](data/images/aurelian-empire-homeland-45e5f79b.jpg "An Aurelian capital seen from its harbour. Notice the scale and order: white stone ministries and domes in ranks above the water, crowned-sun banners, standardised grey steel warships at the quays, a rail yard feeding the docks, and lighthouses marking every approach.")

Aurelian **ships** follow the same logic. Warships are large, disciplined, imposing and purpose-built, and they look alike on purpose. Where a Vardic ship is a signature, an Aurelian one is a statement of institutional power: there are many more where this came from.

## Dress and Rank

Aurelian clothing values fit, maintenance, regulation and institutional identity: **tailored coats**, **high collars**, **polished boots**, **clear rank insignia**, standardised uniforms, formal naval dress and carefully kept equipment.

Roles are meant to be told apart at a glance. An officer, a clerk, an engineer, a doctor, a sailor and an aristocrat should never look identical. But all of them should look like they come from the same place, and that the place has standards.

![Aurelian clothing: commoner, diplomat, soldier and Gate Expeditioner](data/images/aurelian-empire-clothing-ef0470e2.jpg "Four Aurelians. A townsperson in well-made, practical clothes with modest imperial trim; a diplomat in navy and cream with ministry insignia and medals; a marine in structured uniform with gold epaulettes and polished equipment; and a Gate Expeditioner in field-ready gear that is still unmistakably Aurelian. Note the ministry badges, the document case, and cuff trims whose patterns show rank, ministry or role.")

Details to notice:

- **Insignia** are precise. Epaulettes, cuff and collar trim, badges and medals tell anyone who knows how to read them exactly who they are dealing with.
- **Ministries** have their own badges and variations, and officials guard the differences carefully.
- **Equipment** is standard issue wherever possible, and kept in a condition that would pass inspection, because sooner or later it will be inspected.

> **Morning inspection in an Imperial Marines barracks**
>
> The sergeant stopped in front of the newest marine and looked at his boots for a long moment.
>
> "When were these last polished?"
>
> "This morning, Sergeant."
>
> "And the buckles?"
>
> "Also this morning, Sergeant."
>
> "And the left one is still a different shade from the right." The sergeant moved on. "Nobody will ever shoot at you because of your buckle, Private. But one day someone will be relying on whether you noticed it."

## Labels, Serial Numbers and Forms

Aurelian machinery is designed for **standard parts**, **labels**, **serial numbers**, **maintenance access**, **interchangeability** and **documentation**. A Vard may personalise a machine. An Aurelian institution wants to know its model number, its repair schedule, the department responsible for it and the code for every replacement part.

The Empire's love of paperwork is the most mocked thing about it, and Aurelians are aware of this. They are also, privately, rather proud of it. Many of their forms exist because something once went badly wrong.

> **An Aurelian quartermaster's office**
>
> "Form 17-C," said the Vesperian engineer, holding it up. "It asks me to certify the thread pitch of every fitting I'm requisitioning. Every single one."
>
> "It does," said the quartermaster.
>
> "Why?"
>
> The quartermaster put down his pen. "Because some years ago, half a squadron was refitted with valves from two different contractors. The threads looked identical. They were not. Nobody had asked." He picked the pen up again. "We found out during a storm."
>
> The engineer looked at the form again, then filled it in.

The result, when it works, is extraordinary. An Aurelian maintenance crew can replace a damaged component in minutes, anywhere in the world, because every fitting is labelled, every part is standard and the manual is where the manual is supposed to be.

## The Aurelian Manner

The ideal Aurelian is **composed**, **prepared**, **reliable**, **polite**, **competent** and **aware of duty**. Emotional restraint is admired.

This does not mean Aurelians feel less than anyone else. It means they value controlling themselves in public and doing what needs doing whatever they happen to feel about it. Aurelian conflict is usually conducted through formal wording, rank, precedent and very carefully phrased disapproval, and Aurelian humour often comes from extreme politeness wrapped around obvious tension.

Tea is part of this. It is not decoration: it is how Aurelians steady themselves, and each other.

> **Aboard a supply tender in heavy weather, as a passenger remembered it**
>
> The ship had been rolling hard for three hours, and one of the boilers had begun to make a noise nobody liked. The engineer went below. The captain stayed on the bridge.
>
> At precisely four o'clock, a steward appeared on the bridge, braced against the doorframe, with a tray.
>
> The captain took her cup without looking away from the sea, drank half of it, and handed it back.
>
> "Thank you, Mr Pell. Tell the engine room theirs is coming, and that I should like to know about that boiler before they drink it."

## What Foreigners Get Wrong

Foreigners often decide that Aurelians are cold, rigid or incapable of improvising. The first is mostly restraint, and the second is mostly preference. The third is simply wrong. Aurelian officers are trained to use judgment within the rules, and the Crowned Sun teaches that duty without judgment is not duty at all. They improvise constantly. They just fill in the form afterwards.
